fields.title: The Second Letter of Peter
fields.subtitle: Petrou B, “Second of Peter”
fields.description: A farewell letter in Peter’s name, written by one who knows he must soon lay aside “this tent of a body”, so that his readers will remember what matters most. God’s divine power has given us every gift that leads to life and godliness, and promises by which we may share in the divine nature; so add to faith goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, affection and love. The apostles were eyewitnesses on the holy mountain, not tellers of clever stories; false teachers will come, and God knows how to rescue the godly; and to the scoffers who ask “Where is this promise of his coming?”, the answer that with the Lord a day is like a thousand years, that he is patient, not wanting anyone to be destroyed, and that we look for new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Second Letter of Peter?
qa.answer: The twenty-second book of the New Testament, a short farewell letter in which Peter, expecting to die soon, reminds his readers of the truth they have received. It urges them to grow in goodness, knowledge and love, warns against false teachers who promise freedom but live in greed and corruption, and answers those who mock the promise of Christ’s return: God’s seeming delay is his patience, giving people time to repent, and the day of the Lord will surely come. It ends with a call to keep growing in the grace and knowledge of Jesus Christ (3:18).

qa.question: Did Peter write 2 Peter?
qa.answer: The letter names “Simeon Peter” as its author, recalls the transfiguration as something he saw, and calls itself his second letter. But its authorship has been questioned since early times: it is rarely quoted before the third century, Eusebius listed it among the books some disputed, and Jerome noted that its style differs from 1 Peter. Many modern scholars think a follower wrote it after Peter’s death, as a last testament in his name; others hold that Peter wrote it, perhaps with a different secretary, shortly before his martyrdom in the mid-60s. The church received it as Scripture after long consideration.

qa.question: What does “a single day is like a thousand years” mean in 2 Peter 3:8?
qa.answer: Peter is answering scoffers who say the promise of Christ’s coming has failed because so much time has passed. Echoing Psalm 90, he says that God does not measure time as people do: “in the Lord’s sight a single day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like a single day.” The point is not a formula for calculating dates, but that the Lord is not slow in keeping his promise. He is being patient, “He does not want anyone to be destroyed, but wants all people to turn back in repentance” (3:9).

qa.question: What does 2 Peter mean by sharing in “the divine nature”?
qa.answer: In 1:3–4 Peter says that God’s divine power has given his people “every gift that leads to life and godliness”, and that through his promises they “may come to share in the divine nature, now that you have escaped the decay that desire has brought into the world.” The Eastern Orthodox churches have treasured the verse as a summary of salvation, God sharing his own life with human beings; Western Christians have more often spoken of union with Christ. All agree that Peter does not mean people become gods in their own right. He goes straight on to the qualities that should grow from this gift, from faith through goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance and godliness to love (1:5–7).

qa.question: Does 2 Peter say the earth will be burned up?
qa.answer: In 3:10 many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, say the earth and its works “will be burned up”. The oldest manuscripts read that they “will be found”, and the Open Word Bible follows them: “the earth and the deeds done on it will be found out”, laid bare before God. Peter does speak of fire: the present heavens and earth “are being held in store for fire” (3:7), and on the day of God “the elements will melt in the heat” (3:12). Christians differ over whether this means the old world is destroyed and replaced or purified and renewed, but Peter’s hope is plain: “new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home” (3:13).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
By his divine power we have been given every gift that leads to life and godliness, through knowing the one who called us by his own glory and goodness. Through these he has given us his promises, precious and greater than any other, so that through them you may come to share in the divine nature, now that you have escaped the decay that desire has brought into the world.

— 2 Peter 1:3–4

Second Peter is a farewell. Its writer knows that he must soon “lay this tent aside”, as the Lord Jesus had shown him, and he writes so that after he is gone his readers will remember what they have been taught. It is a short letter with three concerns: grow in the knowledge of Christ; do not be led astray by false teachers; and do not give up waiting for the Lord’s return because it seems slow in coming.

Who wrote it?

The letter names its author as “Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ”. It speaks as Peter: he heard the voice from heaven on the holy mountain at the transfiguration, he expects to die soon, and this is his “second letter” to the same readers.

Even so, no book of the New Testament has had its authorship questioned so long. It is hardly quoted in the second century. Origen in the third century knew that some doubted it, and Eusebius in the fourth listed it among the books spoken against, though known to many. Jerome noted that many thought it was not Peter’s because its style differs from that of 1 Peter, and suggested Peter had used a different secretary. Many modern scholars think it was written after Peter’s death, around AD 80–130, by a follower who set down his teaching in the form of a last testament, a kind of writing well known at the time. Others hold that Peter wrote it, perhaps with help, shortly before his martyrdom in the mid-60s. The church, after long weighing, received it as Scripture, and it has been read as such ever since.

Readers also notice that much of chapter 2 is very close to the Letter of Jude, so close that one has surely drawn on the other, or both on a common source.

The shape of the letter

  • Chapter 1: growing in the knowledge of Christ. God’s gifts and promises, the qualities faith should add, and the sure word of the apostles and prophets.
  • Chapter 2: false teachers. Their greed and arrogance, God’s judgment in the past, and the misery of turning back.
  • Chapter 3: the day of the Lord. The scoffers’ question, God’s patience, new heavens and a new earth, and a closing call to grow.

Faith, goodness, love

The letter opens with breathtaking promises. Through knowing Christ, God has given his people everything they need for life and godliness, so that they may “come to share in the divine nature”. The Eastern Orthodox churches have treasured this verse as a summary of salvation: God became human so that human beings might share in his life. Western Christians have spoken more often of union with Christ, and all agree that Peter does not mean people become gods in their own right, but that they share God’s life, free at last from the decay that desire has brought into the world.

Gifts like that call for effort, and Peter sets out a ladder of qualities, each built on the one before:

This is why you must put every effort into this: let your faith provide goodness, and goodness knowledge, knowledge self-control, self-control endurance, endurance godliness, godliness affection for your fellow believers, and that affection love.

— 2 Peter 1:5–7

The ladder begins in faith and ends in love. It is not a way of earning God’s favour; it is how his gifts become fruitful. “So, brothers and sisters, work even harder to make sure that God’s call and choice of you stand firm”.

Not clever stories

Peter’s teaching rests on what he saw. The message of Christ’s power and coming is not made up: he was on the mountain, he saw Christ’s greatness and heard the Father’s voice. And alongside the apostles’ witness stands the word of the prophets, “like a lamp that shines in a murky place, until the day breaks and the morning star rises in your hearts.” No prophecy came because a human being willed it; “rather, people spoke from God as the Holy Spirit bore them along.” Christians have often turned to these verses in thinking about the inspiration of Scripture.

False teachers

Chapter 2 is the letter’s sternest. False teachers will arise in the church as false prophets arose in Israel, greedy, arrogant, promising freedom while “they themselves are slaves of corruption.” Peter reminds his readers of God’s judgments in the past, on rebellious angels, on the ancient world in the flood and on Sodom and Gomorrah, but also of his rescues: Noah kept safe, and Lot, the righteous man, delivered. The lesson cuts both ways: “the Lord knows how to rescue those who are godly from their trials”. The chapter closes with the misery of those who have known the way of righteousness and turned from it.

Where is this promise?

Then the scoffers’ question. “Where is this promise of his coming?” Everything goes on as it always has. Peter answers in three ways. The world has not always gone on unchanged: God’s word made it and God’s word brought the flood. God does not measure time as we do. And the delay is not slowness but mercy:

But you, dear friends, must not overlook this one thing: in the Lord’s sight a single day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like a single day. The Lord is not delaying the promise, as some people think of delay. Rather, he is being patient with you. He does not want anyone to be destroyed, but wants all people to turn back in repentance.

— 2 Peter 3:8–9

The day will come, unexpectedly, like a thief. Christians understand its fire differently, as the destruction of the present world, as its purifying and renewal, or as the laying bare of all things before God. But Peter’s concern is not to satisfy curiosity. It is to ask what kind of people his readers ought to be, and to lift their eyes to “new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home.”

The letter ends with a remarkable mention of Paul, “our dear brother”, who wrote with the wisdom God gave him. “Some things in them are hard to grasp,” Peter says of his letters, and untaught people bend them out of shape, “as they bend the other Scriptures”. It is one of the earliest signs that Paul’s letters were being read alongside the Scriptures of Israel.

How to read 2 Peter

Read it as a last testament, the words of a man setting his affairs in order and leaving his friends what matters most. Read it alongside Jude, to see how the two letters use the same warnings. And notice how it begins and ends in the same place, with growing in grace and in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in 2 Peter are worth knowing about.

“Our God and Savior Jesus Christ.” In 1:1 the translation reads both titles as belonging to Jesus, so that the letter calls him God from its first sentence.

Tartarus. In 2:4 Peter uses a Greek name for the deepest place of punishment, where the rebellious angels are held. The translation keeps the word “Tartarus” rather than flattening it to “hell”.

“Found out.” In 3:10 many later manuscripts say the earth and its works “will be burned up”. The oldest read that they “will be found”, and the translation follows them: the earth and the deeds done on it “will be found out”, laid bare before God.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: 2 Peter 1
fields.body_html:
Greeting

1From Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who, through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ, have received a faith that is worth just as much as our own. 2May you have grace and peace in ever greater measure as you know God and Jesus our Lord.

Grow in what God has given

3By his divine power we have been given every gift that leads to life and godliness, through knowing the one who called us by his own glory and goodness. 4Through these he has given us his promises, precious and greater than any other, so that through them you may come to share in the divine nature, now that you have escaped the decay that desire has brought into the world. 5This is why you must put every effort into this: let your faith provide goodness, and goodness knowledge, 6knowledge self-control, self-control endurance, endurance godliness, 7godliness affection for your fellow believers, and that affection love. 8For when these things are yours in growing measure, they will not leave you useless or without fruit in knowing our Lord Jesus Christ. 9Anyone who lacks them cannot see what is ahead and is as good as blind; they have forgotten that they were made clean from the sins of the past. 10So, brothers and sisters, work even harder to make sure that God’s call and choice of you stand firm; for as you do these things you will never trip and fall. 11This is how you will be given a full and generous welcome into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ.

Peter’s reminder before his death

12So I will keep on reminding you of these things, though you already know them and stand firm in the truth that has come to you. 13While I still live in this tent of a body, I think it right to keep you awake by reminding you, 14because I know that I must soon lay this tent aside, as our Lord Jesus Christ has shown me. 15And I will see to it that after I am gone you will be able to recall these things whenever you need them.

Eyewitnesses of his majesty

16When we told you about the power of our Lord Jesus Christ and his coming, we were not passing on clever stories that people had made up. We had seen his greatness with our own eyes. 17Honor and glory were given to him by God the Father, when these words came to him from the Majestic Glory: “This is my dearly loved Son; I take delight in him.” 18We heard that voice ourselves as it came from heaven, while we were there with him on the holy mountain. 19So the message of the prophets is all the more certain for us. You are right to keep your eyes on it, like a lamp that shines in a murky place, until the day breaks and the morning star rises in your hearts. 20Know this first and foremost: no prophecy in Scripture arises from anyone’s own interpretation, 21for no prophecy ever came because a human being willed it; rather, people spoke from God as the Holy Spirit bore them along.
fields.summary: Peter urges believers to grow in faith, goodness, knowledge and love, building on what God has given. Before his death he reminds them that the apostles were eyewitnesses of the majesty of Jesus on the holy mountain, and that prophecy comes from God.

fields.title: 2 Peter 2
fields.body_html:
False teachers among you

1In the past there were false prophets among the people of Israel, and in the same way there will be false teachers among you. They will quietly bring in teachings that lead to destruction, and they will even disown the Master who bought them. So they will bring swift destruction on themselves. 2Many people will follow their shameless ways, and because of them the way of truth will be slandered. 3In their greed they will make money out of you with stories they have invented. But the judgment passed on them long ago has not been sitting idle, and their destruction has not fallen asleep.

God rescues the godly and judges the wicked

4God did not spare the angels who sinned. He threw them down into Tartarus and handed them over to chains of deepest darkness, where they are held for judgment. 5Nor did he spare the ancient world. When he brought the flood on a world of ungodly people, he kept Noah safe with seven others, Noah who proclaimed righteousness. 6He condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ruin and burned them to ashes, and made them an example of what is coming to the ungodly. 7But he rescued Lot, a righteous man who was worn down by the shameless conduct of lawless people. 8Living among them day after day, that righteous man tormented his righteous soul over the lawless deeds he saw and heard. 9If God did all this, then clearly the Lord knows how to rescue those who are godly from their trials, and how to hold the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment, 10above all those who chase after the flesh with its defiling desires and who look down on the Lord’s authority.

What the false teachers are like

Reckless and arrogant, they are not afraid to slander the glorious ones, 11when even angels, who are greater in strength and power, do not bring a slanderous judgment against them. 12But these people are like animals that cannot reason, ruled by instinct, born to be caught and killed. They slander what they do not understand, and like those animals they too will be destroyed, 13suffering harm as payment for the harm they have done. They think it a pleasure to indulge themselves in broad daylight. They are stains and blemishes, enjoying their deceptions while they eat with you at your meals. 14Their eyes are always on the lookout for adultery and never have enough of sin. They lure people who are not yet steady. They have practiced greed until their hearts are skilled in it. They are people under a curse! 15They have abandoned the straight road and lost their way, following the road of Balaam son of Bosor, who loved the pay he could get for doing wrong. 16But he was confronted with his own lawbreaking. A donkey, which has no power of speech, talked in a human voice and stopped the prophet in his madness.

Promising freedom, slaves of corruption

17These people are springs that have run dry, mists chased along by a squall. The blackest darkness is being kept for them. 18They speak big, empty words, and with the flesh and its shameless desires as bait they lure people who are only just getting away from those who are living astray. 19They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For anyone who is overcome by something has become its slave. 20For if they have escaped the filth of the world by knowing the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and then get tangled up in it again and overcome, they end up worse off than they were at the start. 21They would have been better off never knowing the way of righteousness than knowing it and then abandoning the holy commandment entrusted to them. 22The true proverb has come true for them: “A dog goes back to what it threw up,” and, “A pig, once washed, goes back to rolling in the mud.”
fields.summary: False teachers will arise among believers, as false prophets did in Israel. God rescued Noah and Lot and judged the wicked, and these teachers, who promise freedom, are themselves slaves of corruption.

fields.title: 2 Peter 3
fields.body_html:
Where is the promise of his coming?

1Dear friends, this is now my second letter to you. In both of them I am trying to rouse your minds to clear thinking by reminding you 2to remember what the holy prophets said long ago, and the command of the Lord and Savior that your apostles passed on to you. 3Above all, understand this: in the last days scoffers will come, full of scorn, living by their own desires. 4They will say, “Where is this promise of his coming? For ever since our ancestors died, everything goes on just as it has from the beginning of creation.” 5They choose to overlook this: long ago, by the word of God, the heavens came into being, and the earth was formed out of water and by means of water. 6By these, water and word, the world of that time was flooded and destroyed. 7But by that same word the present heavens and earth are being held in store for fire. They are kept for the day when ungodly people will be judged and destroyed.

The Lord is patient

8But you, dear friends, must not overlook this one thing: in the Lord’s sight a single day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like a single day. 9The Lord is not delaying the promise, as some people think of delay. Rather, he is being patient with you. He does not want anyone to be destroyed, but wants all people to turn back in repentance. 10But the day of the Lord will come like a thief. On that day the heavens will vanish with a rushing sound, the elements will be set ablaze and break apart, and the earth and the deeds done on it will be found out.

Waiting for the day of God

11Since everything is to be dissolved in this way, think what sort of people you ought to be! Live holy and godly lives, 12as you wait for the coming of the day of God and hurry it on. That day will set the heavens on fire and dissolve them, and the elements will melt in the heat. 13But we are looking forward to what he promised: new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home.

Be found at peace

14So, dear friends, while you wait for these things, work hard to be found by him spotless and without fault, and at peace. 15Regard our Lord’s patience as salvation. Paul, our dear brother, wrote to you about this too, with the wisdom God gave him. 16He does so in all his letters when he speaks of these things. Some things in them are hard to grasp, and people who are untaught and unsteady bend them out of shape, as they bend the other Scriptures, and so bring about their own destruction. 17So, dear friends, since you have been told this in advance, be on your guard. Do not let the error of lawless people sweep you along and knock you off your own firm footing. 18Instead, keep growing in the grace that comes from our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and in knowing him. May glory be his, both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.
fields.summary: Scoffers will ask where the promised coming of the Lord is, but the Lord is patient, not wanting anyone to perish. The day of the Lord will come like a thief, so believers must live holy lives and be found at peace.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
So, dear friends, since you have been told this in advance, be on your guard. Do not let the error of lawless people sweep you along and knock you off your own firm footing. Instead, keep growing in the grace that comes from our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and in knowing him. May glory be his, both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.

— 2 Peter 3:17–18

Second Peter ends where it began. Its first chapter called its readers to grow, adding goodness, knowledge and love to their faith; its last sentence calls them to keep growing in grace and in knowing Christ. Between the two stand the false teachers and the scoffers. The letter’s answer to both is not simply to argue with them, but to grow so deep in Christ that their words lose their pull.

The question the letter leaves

The question 2 Peter leaves is what to do with the waiting. Its readers had been told the Lord was coming, and he had not come, and some were laughing at them. Peter does not set a date. He tells them that God’s patience is itself a kind of salvation, giving time for people to turn back, and that the right response to the waiting is a holy and godly life. “Regard our Lord’s patience as salvation.”

Where to go from here

A few places in this library to read further:

  • On growing in grace (3:18). J. C. Ryle’s chapter Growth, in Holiness; Charles G. Finney’s Growth in Grace, the last of his Lectures on Revivals of Religion; and two sermons on the verse, A. W. Tozer’s How to Grow in Grace and A. B. Simpson’s Spiritual Growth.
  • On God’s call and choice (1:10). Ryle’s Election, in Old Paths.
  • On the prophetic word (1:19–21). Simpson’s The Holy Spirit in the Epistles of Peter, in The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High, Part II; and R. A. Torrey’s chapter on inspiration in The Fundamental Doctrines of the Christian Faith.
  • On holy living as we wait (3:11). Andrew Murray’s Holiness and Heaven, the last reading in Holy in Christ.
  • On sharing the divine nature (1:4). Athanasius of Alexandria’s On the Incarnation, the classic account of the Word made flesh to restore human beings to God’s life.
  • On how the letter was received. Eusebius of Caesarea’s The Church History, which records which books the early churches accepted and which they still weighed.

Every reference to 2 Peter in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather what the great writers of the church have said about each passage.

But the best next step may be the one Peter asks for: to remember. He wrote so that his readers could recall these things whenever they needed them. Read the letter again when the waiting feels long, and hold on to its promise:

But we are looking forward to what he promised: new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home.

— 2 Peter 3:13
